claim: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) represents the most prevalent form of inherited intellectual disability.
source: The fragile X syndrome (FXS) represents the most prevalent form of inherited intellectual disability and is the first monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about FXS prevalence.

claim: FXS is the first monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder.
source: The fragile X syndrome (FXS) represents the most prevalent form of inherited intellectual disability and is the first monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about FXS and autism.

claim: FXS results from the absence of the RNA-binding protein FMRP (fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein).
source: FXS results from the absence of the RNA-binding protein FMRP (fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the molecular cause of FXS.

claim: The absence of FMRP leads to delayed neuronal migration in postnatal rostral migratory stream (RMS) neurons in Fmr1-null mice.
source: Using live imaging of postnatal rostral migratory stream (RMS) neurons in Fmr1-null mice, we observed that the absence of FMRP leads to delayed neuronal migration and altered trajectory, associated with defects of centrosomal movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging experiments performed in the study.

claim: The absence of FMRP leads to altered trajectory in postnatal RMS neurons in Fmr1-null mice.
source: Using live imaging of postnatal rostral migratory stream (RMS) neurons in Fmr1-null mice, we observed that the absence of FMRP leads to delayed neuronal migration and altered trajectory, associated with defects of centrosomal movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging experiments performed in the study.

claim: The absence of FMRP is associated with defects of centrosomal movement in postnatal RMS neurons.
source: Using live imaging of postnatal rostral migratory stream (RMS) neurons in Fmr1-null mice, we observed that the absence of FMRP leads to delayed neuronal migration and altered trajectory, associated with defects of centrosomal movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging experiments performed in the study.

claim: The migratory defects caused by FMRP absence are cell-autonomous.
source: RNA-interference-induced knockdown of Fmr1 shows that these migratory defects are cell-autonomous.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA interference experiments performed in the study.

claim: Microtubule-associated protein 1B (MAP1B) is the primary Fmrp mRNA target implicated in migratory defects.
source: Notably, the primary Fmrp mRNA target implicated in these migratory defects is microtubule-associated protein 1B (MAP1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing MAP1B's role in the observed phenotypes.

claim: Knocking down MAP1B expression effectively rescued most of the observed migratory defects.
source: Knocking down MAP1B expression effectively rescued most of the observed migratory defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by MAP1B knockdown rescue experiments performed in the study.

claim: The absence of FMRP induces defects in the cage of microtubules surrounding the nucleus of migrating neurons.
source: Finally, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms at play by demonstrating that the absence of FMRP induces defects in the cage of microtubules surrounding the nucleus of migrating neurons, which is rescued by MAP1B knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by microtubule imaging experiments performed in the study.

claim: Defects in the microtubule cage caused by FMRP absence are rescued by MAP1B knockdown.
source: Finally, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms at play by demonstrating that the absence of FMRP induces defects in the cage of microtubules surrounding the nucleus of migrating neurons, which is rescued by MAP1B knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments with MAP1B knockdown performed in the study.

claim: FXS is the most common cause of inherited intellectual disability.
source: The fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most common cause of inherited intellectual disability and a leading cause of autism spectrum disorder.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about FXS.

claim: FXS is a leading cause of autism spectrum disorder.
source: The fragile X syndrome (FXS) is the most common cause of inherited intellectual disability and a leading cause of autism spectrum disorder.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about FXS and autism.

claim: FXS is due to the silencing of the gene FMR1 and loss of the encoded protein, FMRP.
source: FXS is due to the silencing of the gene FMR1 and loss of the encoded protein, FMRP (fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein) (Davis and Broadie, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Davis and Broadie, 2017.

claim: FMRP is an ubiquitous RNA-binding protein with high level of expression in the central nervous system.
source: FMRP is an ubiquitous RNA-binding protein, with high level of expression in the central nervous system (Gholizadeh et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gholizadeh et al., 2015.

claim: FMRP is a general regulator of RNA metabolism and especially of mRNA local translation in neurons.
source: It is a general regulator of RNA metabolism and especially of mRNA local translation in neurons (Banerjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Banerjee et al., 2018.

claim: FMRP cognate mRNA targets are numerous and diverse, including mRNAs encoding proteins involved in neuronal plasticity like CamKIIα and cytoskeletal proteins like MAP1B.
source: Its cognate mRNA targets are numerous and diverse, including mRNAs encoding proteins involved in neuronal plasticity like CamKIIα (calcium calmodulin-dependent kinase II) and cytoskeletal proteins like microtubule-associated protein 1B (MAP1B) (Ascano et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Maurin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ascano et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Maurin et al., 2018.

claim: Fmr1-null mice are the murine model of FXS.
source: Fmr1-null mice are the murine model of FXS and have allowed characterization of numerous neurodevelopmental and plasticity defects consecutive to the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mouse model used in FXS research.

claim: Fmr1-null mice have allowed characterization of numerous neurodevelopmental and plasticity defects consecutive to the absence of FMRP.
source: Fmr1-null mice are the murine model of FXS and have allowed characterization of numerous neurodevelopmental and plasticity defects consecutive to the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of the mouse model, supported by the broader literature.

claim: FMRP plays an essential role in the differentiation and learning-induced structural plasticity of adult-generated olfactory bulb interneurons.
source: We previously showed the essential role of FMRP in the differentiation and learning-induced structural plasticity of adult-generated olfactory bulb interneurons (Scotto-Lomassese et al., 2011; Daroles et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Scotto-Lomassese et al., 2011; Daroles et al., 2016).

claim: Neuronal migration is a crucial step for the establishment of neuronal circuitry, orchestrating the relocation of neurons from their birthplace to their final destination for differentiation.
source: Neuronal migration is a crucial step for the establishment of neuronal circuitry, orchestrating the relocation of neurons from their birthplace to their final destination for differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal migration in neurodevelopment.

claim: Migration defects lead to severe brain pathologies including lissencephaly and cortical heterotopia and may contribute to psychiatric disorders.
source: Migration defects lead to severe brain pathologies including lissencephaly and cortical heterotopia and may contribute to psychiatric disorders (Romero et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Romero et al., 2018.

claim: Migration in the human infant brain appears to be even more extended than anticipated from the rodent data.
source: Interestingly, migration in the human infant brain appears to be even more extended than anticipated from the rodent data (Sanai et al., 2011; Paredes et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sanai et al., 2011; Paredes et al., 2016.

claim: Periventricular heterotopia has been documented in two individuals with FXS.
source: In addition, periventricular heterotopia has been documented in two individuals with FXS, implying a potential role for FMRP in migration (Moro et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moro et al., 2006.

claim: Periventricular heterotopia in FXS individuals implies a potential role for FMRP in migration.
source: In addition, periventricular heterotopia has been documented in two individuals with FXS, implying a potential role for FMRP in migration (Moro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of heterotopia in FXS patients.

claim: In Fmr1-null mice, radially migrating embryonic glutamatergic cortical neurons display a defect in the multipolar to bipolar transition.
source: Importantly, in Fmr1-null mice, radially migrating embryonic glutamatergic cortical neurons display a defect in the multipolar to bipolar transition (La Fata et al., 2014), a critical change of polarity taking place before the initiation of the movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to La Fata et al., 2014.

claim: The multipolar to bipolar transition is a critical change of polarity taking place before the initiation of neuronal movement.
source: Importantly, in Fmr1-null mice, radially migrating embryonic glutamatergic cortical neurons display a defect in the multipolar to bipolar transition (La Fata et al., 2014), a critical change of polarity taking place before the initiation of the movement.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal migration, contextualized by the citation.

claim: N-cadherin is the key Fmrp target mRNA involved in the multipolar to bipolar transition defect.
source: The key Fmrp target mRNA involved in this process is N-cadherin, downregulated in the Fmr1 mutants and whose overexpression rescued the migratory phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from La Fata et al., 2014, as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: N-cadherin is downregulated in Fmr1 mutants.
source: The key Fmrp target mRNA involved in this process is N-cadherin, downregulated in the Fmr1 mutants and whose overexpression rescued the migratory phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from La Fata et al., 2014, as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: Overexpression of N-cadherin rescued the migratory phenotype in Fmr1 mutants.
source: The key Fmrp target mRNA involved in this process is N-cadherin, downregulated in the Fmr1 mutants and whose overexpression rescued the migratory phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from La Fata et al., 2014, as referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: Both FMRP overexpression and knockdown lead to the misplacement of cortical glutamatergic neurons.
source: Additionally, both FMRP overexpression or knockdown (KD) lead to the misplacement of cortical glutamatergic neurons, also potentially underscoring its role in radial embryonic migration (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Postnatal neuronal migration in the absence of FMRP has not been studied.
source: However, to our knowledge, postnatal neuronal migration in the absence of FMRP has not been studied so far and the dynamics of mutated Fmr1 neurons have yet to be comprehensively analyzed.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: The dynamics of mutated Fmr1 neurons have yet to be comprehensively analyzed.
source: However, to our knowledge, postnatal neuronal migration in the absence of FMRP has not been studied so far and the dynamics of mutated Fmr1 neurons have yet to be comprehensively analyzed.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: Migrating neurons in Fmr1-null mice exhibit a distinctive pattern of slowed-down and erratic migration.
source: Migrating neurons in Fmr1-null mice exhibit a distinctive pattern of slowed-down and erratic migration, accompanied by alterations of centrosome movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Migrating neurons in Fmr1-null mice exhibit alterations of centrosome movement.
source: Migrating neurons in Fmr1-null mice exhibit a distinctive pattern of slowed-down and erratic migration, accompanied by alterations of centrosome movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The migratory defects in Fmr1-null mice are cell-autonomous, as evidenced by their recapitulation through RNA-interference-induced Fmr1 KD.
source: Notably, these defects are cell-autonomous, as evidenced by their recapitulation through RNA-interference-induced Fmr1 KD.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA interference experiments performed in the study.

claim: MAP1B is a microtubule-associated protein that plays a crucial role in the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics within neurons.
source: MAP1B is a microtubule-associated protein that plays a crucial role in the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics within neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAP1B function.

claim: MAP1B is instrumental in brain development.
source: It is instrumental in brain development (Villarroel-Campos and Gonzalez-Billault, 2014) including neuronal migration (Yang et al., 2012; González-Billault et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Billault et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Villarroel-Campos and Gonzalez-Billault, 2014.

claim: MAP1B is instrumental in neuronal migration.
source: It is instrumental in brain development (Villarroel-Campos and Gonzalez-Billault, 2014) including neuronal migration (Yang et al., 2012; González-Billault et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Billault et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2012; González-Billault et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Billault et al., 2004.

claim: Elevated levels of MAP1B were detected in the mutated RMS.
source: Indeed, elevated levels of MAP1B were detected in the mutated RMS, and the KD-induced downregulation of MAP1B successfully rescued most migration defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study (western blot analysis).

claim: KD-induced downregulation of MAP1B successfully rescued most migration defects.
source: Indeed, elevated levels of MAP1B were detected in the mutated RMS, and the KD-induced downregulation of MAP1B successfully rescued most migration defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments performed in the study.

claim: The microtubular cage surrounding the nucleus of migrating neurons is disrupted in the absence of FMRP.
source: Finally, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying these migratory defects, by showing that the microtubular cage surrounding the nucleus of migrating neurons is disrupted in the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This claim is supported by microtubule imaging experiments performed in the study.

claim: The microtubular cage abnormality is rescued by MAP1B KD.
source: Importantly, this abnormality is rescued by MAP1B KD, shedding light on a previously undiscovered role for the FMRP/MAP1B duo in regulating proper tangential migration at the microtubular level.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments performed in the study.

claim: The FMRP/MAP1B duo has a previously undiscovered role in regulating proper tangential migration at the microtubular level.
source: Importantly, this abnormality is rescued by MAP1B KD, shedding light on a previously undiscovered role for the FMRP/MAP1B duo in regulating proper tangential migration at the microtubular level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: A massive number of neuroblasts are constantly produced in the ventricular/subventricular zone (V/SVZ) and migrate over a long distance along the RMS to the olfactory bulb (OB).
source: A massive number of neuroblasts are constantly produced in the ventricular/subventricular zone (V/SVZ) and migrate over a long distance along the RMS to the olfactory bulb (OB) (Lim and Alvarez-Buylla, 2016; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lim and Alvarez-Buylla, 2016 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: RMS neurons display a cyclic saltatory mode of migration, in which the nucleus and centrosome move forward in a 'two-stroke' cycle.
source: They display a cyclic saltatory mode of migration, in which the nucleus and centrosome move forward in a 'two-stroke' cycle (Bellion et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bellion et al., 2005.

claim: The centrosome moves first within a swelling in the leading process, termed centrokinesis (CK), followed by movement of the nucleus, referred to as nucleokinesis (NK).
source: The centrosome moves first within a swelling in the leading process, termed here centrokinesis (CK) followed by movement of the nucleus, referred to as nucleokinesis (NK) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the migration cycle, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: FMRP is expressed in most neurons of the brain.
source: FMRP is expressed in most neurons of the brain (Gholizadeh et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gholizadeh et al., 2015.

claim: FMRP is strongly expressed in the RMS, where most neurons appear labeled.
source: Accordingly, immunostaining for FMRP reveals that FMRP is strongly expressed in the RMS, where most neurons appear labeled (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In individual GFP-positive neurons, FMRP labeling appears as a discrete and punctate staining visible mainly in the cytoplasm both at the rear of the neuron and in the leading process.
source: In individual GFP-positive neurons, FMRP labeling appears as a discrete and punctate staining visible mainly in the cytoplasm both at the rear of the neuron and in the leading process (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FMRP labeling appeared as a granular staining similarly visible around the nucleus, in the swelling and in the leading process in V/SVZ explant cultures.
source: FMRP labeling appeared as a granular staining similarly visible around the nucleus, in the swelling and in the leading process.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data from V/SVZ explant cultures shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons display a slowed-down migration.
source: Fmr1-null neurons display a slowed-down migration, an increased pausing time, a more sinuous trajectory, and a defective directionality (Figure 2A–D from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons display an increased pausing time.
source: Fmr1-null neurons display a slowed-down migration, an increased pausing time, a more sinuous trajectory, and a defective directionality (Figure 2A–D from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons display a more sinuous trajectory.
source: Fmr1-null neurons display a slowed-down migration, an increased pausing time, a more sinuous trajectory, and a defective directionality (Figure 2A–D from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons display a defective directionality.
source: Fmr1-null neurons display a slowed-down migration, an increased pausing time, a more sinuous trajectory, and a defective directionality (Figure 2A–D from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The NK is less frequent in Fmr1-null neurons.
source: Additionally, the NK is less frequent and the mean distance per NK is reduced (Figure 2E and F from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The mean distance per NK is reduced in Fmr1-null neurons.
source: Additionally, the NK is less frequent and the mean distance per NK is reduced (Figure 2E and F from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The centrosome plays a crucial role in neuronal migration.
source: Given the crucial role of the centrosome in neuronal migration (Higginbotham and Gleeson, 2007), we analyzed its dynamics by performing co-electroporation of GFP and centrin-RFP in Fmr1-null and control neonate mice in order to co-label migrating neurons and their centrosome (Figure 3—video 1 from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Higginbotham and Gleeson, 2007.

claim: The CK is slowed down in Fmr1-null neurons, as compared to controls.
source: The CK is slowed down and less frequent in Fmr1-null neurons, as compared to controls (Figure 3A and B from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The CK is less frequent in Fmr1-null neurons, as compared to controls.
source: The CK is slowed down and less frequent in Fmr1-null neurons, as compared to controls (Figure 3A and B from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A CK leading to a subsequent NK was defined as an efficient CK, as opposed to a CK not leading to an NK.
source: A CK leading to a subsequent NK was defined as an efficient CK, as opposed to a CK not leading to an NK.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: CK efficiency is reduced in Fmr1-null neurons as compared to controls.
source: CK efficiency is reduced in Fmr1-null neurons as compared to controls (Figure 3C from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: While all neurons electroporated by the control miRNeg-GFP were FMRP immunoreactive, this was reduced to 36% in miRFmr1-GFP electroporated neurons.
source: While all neurons electroporated by the control miRNeg-GFP were FMRP immunoreactive, this was reduced to 36% in miRFmr1-GFP electroporated neurons (Chi2 test, p-value = 0.01; miRNeg condition: N=3, n=15; miRFmr1 condition: N=3, n=14).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and statistical analysis.

claim: Fmr1 KD is sufficient to mostly recapitulate the migratory phenotype described in Fmr1-null mutants.
source: Analysis of migration and centrosome dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 from https://osf.io/eqhzx) showed that Fmr1 KD is sufficient to mostly recapitulate the migratory phenotype described in Fmr1-null mutants, revealing that FMRP cell-autonomously regulates neuronal migration (Kruskal-Wallis followed by Dunn's post hoc analysis on the four genotypes).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA interference experiments and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: FMRP cell-autonomously regulates neuronal migration.
source: Analysis of migration and centrosome dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 from https://osf.io/eqhzx) showed that Fmr1 KD is sufficient to mostly recapitulate the migratory phenotype described in Fmr1-null mutants, revealing that FMRP cell-autonomously regulates neuronal migration (Kruskal-Wallis followed by Dunn's post hoc analysis on the four genotypes).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA interference experiments demonstrating cell-autonomous effects.

claim: The directionality defect might not be cell-autonomous in Fmr1-null mutants but rather a consequence of the mutated environment.
source: This suggests that this defect might not be cell-autonomous in Fmr1-null mutants but rather a consequence of the mutated environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between KD and null mutant phenotypes.

claim: The more pronounced directionality defect in the KD could be indicative of a lack of compensation in the acute KD context.
source: This more pronounced directionality defect in the KD could be indicative of a lack of compensation in the acute KD context.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed difference between KD and null mutant phenotypes.

claim: FMRP is cell-autonomously necessary for the proper neuronal migration of RMS neurons.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that FMRP is cell-autonomously necessary for the proper neuronal migration of RMS neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: MAP1B is a neuron-specific microtubule-associated protein widely expressed in the developing CNS with crucial roles in diverse steps of neural development including neuronal migration.
source: MAP1B is a neuron-specific microtubule-associated protein widely expressed in the developing CNS with crucial roles in diverse steps of neural development including neuronal migration (Yang et al., 2012; González-Billault et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Billault et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2012; González-Billault et al., 2005; Gonzalez-Billault et al., 2004.

claim: MAP1B is expressed in the RMS, with most neurons appearing labeled.
source: Immunostaining of the RMS revealed MAP1B expression, with most neurons appearing labeled (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MAP1B subcellular staining is consistent with labeling of microtubules both around the nucleus and in the leading process.
source: MAP1B subcellular staining is consistent with labeling of microtubules both around the nucleus and in the leading process (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunostaining of individualized neurons migrating in Matrigel showed MAP1B labeling around the nucleus and in the leading process, with occasional microtubule bundles.
source: Immunostaining of individualized neurons migrating in Matrigel similarly showed a labeling around the nucleus and in the leading process, with occasional microtubule bundles (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MAP1B is a well-described Fmrp mRNA target.
source: MAP1B is a well-described Fmrp mRNA target (Zhang et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Brown et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Brown et al., 2001.

claim: FMRP is a repressor of Map1b mRNA translation.
source: As FMRP is a repressor of Map1b mRNA translation (Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2004), the overall level of MAP1B typically appears increased in an Fmr1-null context (Lu et al., 2004; Hou et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2004.

claim: The overall level of MAP1B typically appears increased in an Fmr1-null context.
source: As FMRP is a repressor of Map1b mRNA translation (Brown et al., 2001; Darnell et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2004), the overall level of MAP1B typically appears increased in an Fmr1-null context (Lu et al., 2004; Hou et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2004; Hou et al., 2006.

claim: MAP1B expression is increased on average by 1.6× in the RMS of Fmr1-null mice compared to controls.
source: Accordingly, the quantification of three independent western blots showed that MAP1B expression is increased on average by 1.6× in the RMS of Fmr1-null mice compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: While all neurons electroporated by the control miRNeg-GFP were MAP1B immunoreactive, this was reduced to 46% in miRMAP1B-GFP electroporated neurons.
source: While all neurons electroporated by the control miRNeg-GFP were MAP1B immunoreactive, this was reduced to 46% in miRMAP1B-GFP electroporated neurons (Chi2 test, p-value <0.001. miRNeg condition: N=4, n=103; miRMap1b condition: N=3, n=113).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and statistical analysis.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of migration speed, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons.
source: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of migration speed, pausing time, NK distance, and frequency, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons (Figure 5A, B, D, E from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of pausing time, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons.
source: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of migration speed, pausing time, NK distance, and frequency, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons (Figure 5A, B, D, E from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of NK distance, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons.
source: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of migration speed, pausing time, NK distance, and frequency, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons (Figure 5A, B, D, E from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of NK frequency, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons.
source: Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP exhibited a complete restoration of migration speed, pausing time, NK distance, and frequency, making them comparable to miRNeg-GFP control neurons (Figure 5A, B, D, E from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The sinuosity of Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP was not rescued.
source: Notably, the sinuosity of Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP was not rescued (Figure 5C from https://osf.io/eqhzx), suggesting that this parameter is MAP1B-independent.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The sinuosity parameter is MAP1B-independent.
source: Notably, the sinuosity of Fmr1-null neurons expressing miRMap1b-GFP was not rescued (Figure 5C from https://osf.io/eqhzx), suggesting that this parameter is MAP1B-independent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of rescue of sinuosity by MAP1B knockdown.

claim: MAP1B is the primary Fmrp mRNA target responsible for regulating neuronal migration.
source: In conclusion, our results demonstrate that MAP1B is the primary Fmrp mRNA target responsible for regulating neuronal migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: In control neurons co-electroporated with mirNeg-GFP, a well-defined cage of DCX-positive microtubule bundles smoothly encircling the nucleus was observed in the vast majority of neurons.
source: In control neurons co-electroporated with mirNeg-GFP, subsequent immunostaining revealed a well-defined cage of DCX-positive microtubule bundles smoothly encircling the nucleus in the vast majority of neurons, consistent with observations in other systems (Figure 6A from https://osf.io/eqhzx; Rivas and Hatten, 1995; Shu et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Rivas and Hatten, 1995; Shu et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2003.

claim: mirFmr1-GFP co-electroporation with DCX-RFP unveiled an aberrant microtubular cage in a majority of neurons.
source: Contrastingly, mirFmr1-GFP co-electroporation with DCX-RFP unveiled an aberrant microtubular cage in a majority of neurons (Figure 6B from https://osf.io/eqhzx).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Disorganized neurons with aberrant microtubular cages exhibited disruptions in the cage (46% of them) or sinuous cages (33%) and sometimes even bundles of microtubules detaching from the nucleus (21%).
source: These disorganized neurons exhibited disruptions in the cage (46% of them) or sinuous cages (33%) and sometimes even bundles of microtubules detaching from the nucleus (21%).
